edition.sessionCovered: Fri, Oct 30 close (Binance hack / gold breaks $4k)
edition.stripNote: Sat 31 Oct. Gold breaks $4,000 — yearly low $3,876. Binance $6.3B hack — largest crypto heist ever. BTC below $77k. Oil rallies on Iran strike reports. Silver crashes below $50. OPEC+ meets Sun. US midterms Tue.
edition.scoreboardCaption: Fri 30 Oct close vs Thu 29 close. Ranked best to worst.
edition.commodleHint: Binance lost $6.3 billion in the largest crypto _____ in history

overview: Gold crashed 3.6% to $3,876 on Friday, decisively breaking the $4,000 support level to hit its lowest point of 2026 — roughly 31% below January's record near $5,608. The sell-off extended Thursday's reaction to September PCE inflation (+0.5% m/m, the hottest since March), with the December rate-hike probability at 87% and 10-year Treasury yields near 5%. Silver plunged 6.2% to $48.90, falling below $50 for the first time since November 2025, while platinum dropped 3.9% to $1,435 and palladium slipped to $982. Oil moved against the precious metals rout: Brent rose 1.4% to $112.33 and WTI jumped 2.1% to $104 after reports that a senior US military commander briefed President Trump on options for renewed strikes on Iran and two tanker incidents raised tensions near the Strait of Hormuz. October's Hormuz shipping attacks hit a record. OPEC+ meets Sunday; US midterms are Tuesday.

The session's other earthquake was the Binance hack: the world's largest crypto exchange confirmed a $6.3 billion security breach in its hot wallets — the biggest digital asset heist in history — with blockchain intelligence firm TRM attributing the attack to North Korea's Lazarus Group. Bitcoin dropped below $77,000 to about $76,800, down roughly 3%, while Ethereum fell to $2,220. Binance suspended all deposits and withdrawals and pledged to cover customer losses. Copper fell 1.7% to $6.48/lb as a broad tech-led equity selloff (Nasdaq −2.9%, S&P 500 −1.8%) pressured industrial metals; October marks copper's first monthly loss since June. Newcastle coal firmed to $152.45 on persistent coal-switching demand as European TTF gas stayed above €100/MWh. Corn eased to 448¢ and soybeans settled at 1,222¢. Chinese lithium carbonate continued sliding, with spot near ¥97,500 — roughly halved from its mid-May peak above ¥200,000.

watchItems.title: Binance $6.3B hack — crypto contagion risk
watchItems.text: The largest crypto exchange heist in history has shaken market confidence. Binance suspended all deposits and withdrawals on Friday and pledged to cover losses, but the breach — attributed to North Korea's Lazarus Group via a compromised engineer's laptop — raises systemic questions about centralised exchange security. Bitcoin fell below $77,000, and approximately $1.5 billion in leveraged crypto bets were unwound. Markets are watching whether the hack triggers broader contagion, regulatory responses, or a flight to decentralised platforms. The previous record was the $1.5 billion Bybit heist in 2025, also attributed to Lazarus.

watchItems.title: US midterm elections November 3
watchItems.text: Tuesday's midterms could reshape Washington's approach to the Iran-Hormuz conflict. Reports indicate a senior US military commander briefed President Trump on options for renewed strikes on Iran after the vote, while VP Vance's letter to Iran's Rezaei has opened a separate diplomatic track that Tehran has so far rejected. Control of Congress affects defence budgets, sanctions authority, and the legislative path for any Iran settlement. The elections also carry implications for crypto regulation in the wake of the Binance hack.

watchItems.title: OPEC+ meets Sunday, November 1
watchItems.text: OPEC+ convenes with Brent above $112, Hormuz attacks at record levels, and oil markets pulled between geopolitical supply risk and macro demand headwinds. The hot PCE print, 87% December hike probability, and elevated real yields threaten demand, while physical supply disruptions from Hormuz and potential US military action on Iran support prices. Whether the group signals a willingness to ease voluntary cuts ahead of Tuesday's midterms will set the tone for crude into year-end.

watchItems.title: Gold below $4,000 — where is support?
watchItems.text: Gold's 3.6% plunge below $4,000 to $3,876 marks a decisive technical breakdown. Standard Chartered's Suki Cooper identifies $3,886 as the next key support, warning that a sustained break could trigger a deeper correction. JPMorgan's Yuxuan Tang sees further near-term downside, projecting 10-year yields at 5.25%–5.50% if the Fed hikes in December. The consensus Reuters poll of 30 analysts still expects gold at $4,495 for 2026, implying the current selloff is overdone — but gold 'will find a solid bottom when rates peak,' not before.

desk.name: Gold
desk.sum: Gold crashed 3.6% to $3,876 on Friday, decisively breaking below the $4,000 support level to set a fresh 2026 low — roughly 31% below January's record near $5,608. The September PCE print at 0.5% m/m continued to ripple through markets a day after release, with the December hike probability at 87% and the 10-year yield near 5%. Standard Chartered sees $3,886 as next support; a break could trigger a deeper correction toward $3,800. JPMorgan expects rates to peak before gold finds a solid floor.

desk.name: Silver
desk.sum: Silver plunged 6.2% to $48.90, falling below $50 for the first time since November 2025. The metal is down about 19% in October, its worst monthly decline in over a year, as rising real yields and expectations of higher-for-longer rates hammered the entire precious metals complex. The gold-silver ratio widened to approximately 79.3, reflecting silver's steeper underperformance.

desk.name: Oil
desk.sum: Brent rose 1.4% to $112.33 and WTI jumped 2.1% to $104 on Friday after reports that a senior US military commander briefed President Trump on options for renewed strikes on Iran. Two tanker incidents near the Strait of Hormuz added to the war-risk premium. Tehran has rejected a Qatari-mediated draft ceasefire proposal. October closed with Hormuz shipping attacks at a record high. Europe has announced plans to release 42 million barrels of oil reserves over the next three months. OPEC+ meets Sunday.

desk.name: Copper
desk.sum: Copper fell 1.7% to $6.48 per pound on Friday, set to post its first monthly loss since June at roughly −2% for October. A broad tech-led equity selloff (Nasdaq −2.9%) weighed on industrial metals alongside AI spending concerns. LME three-month copper touched a one-week low of $14,133 per tonne. Chile's September copper output fell 15.1% year-on-year to 387,870 tonnes, supporting the tightness narrative, but macro headwinds dominated.

desk.name: Coal
desk.sum: Newcastle coal firmed to $152.45, its highest level since October 2024, gaining about 2.6% over the past four weeks. European TTF natural gas remaining above €100 per MWh continues to support coal-switching economics in Asia and Europe. Indonesia's export restrictions and the Hormuz disruption to Qatari LNG flows keep the supply side tight. An Australian court rejected a coal mine expansion appeal.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.sum: Platinum dropped 3.9% to $1,435 on Friday — extending its brutal October decline to about 17%. The metal hit a 52-week low earlier in the week after breaching $1,500. Rising real yields and the hot PCE print crushed rate-sensitive metals. WPIC now expects a 265,000-ounce surplus in 2026, and the December hike probability at 87% adds further downward pressure. The metal is roughly 51% below its January record of $2,924.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.sum: Palladium fell 2.2% to $982, dropping below the psychologically important $1,000 level. The metal is down about 23% on the month, the worst performer on the desk in percentage terms. Platinum substitution in gasoline catalysts and growing EV market share continue to structurally weigh on demand. Aerospace and superalloy end-uses provide a floor.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: ~10 transits/day vs 85 pre-war · 35+ attacks in Oct
desk.sum: October closed with the highest monthly total of shipping attacks in the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began in February. Cargo vessel transits have dropped to about 10 per day — down from roughly 85 pre-war — and no large ships have passed through since early September. A senior US military commander briefed President Trump on options for renewed strikes on Iran, and VP Vance's letter to Iran's Rezaei was met with Tehran calling the ceasefire proposal 'unacceptable.' UKMTO has logged over 150 conflict-related incidents since the crisis began. OPEC+ meets Sunday.

desk.name: Corn
desk.sum: December corn eased to 448 cents on Friday, consolidating around the $4.50 level. Managed money still holds substantial short positions. The US corn harvest is nearing completion at roughly the five-year average pace. ADMIS notes that corn has fallen $0.08 for the week as harvest pressure and the strong dollar weigh on prices.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.sum: December wheat was essentially flat at 598 cents on Friday, ending October down about 16%. ADMIS reports wheat fell $0.17 to $0.21 across the three classes for the week. Record managed-money short positions and adequate global supply continue to weigh on prices. Winter wheat planting remains on schedule across the US Southern Plains.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.sum: January soybeans edged up 0.1% to 1,222 cents on Friday, finding modest support even as the month ended down about 5%. The US harvest continues to run ahead of the five-year average, pointing to a large crop. Near-term Chinese buying interest provided a floor, but Brazilian production estimates remain robust.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.sum: Bitcoin plunged below $77,000 to about $76,800 on Friday after Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, confirmed a $6.3 billion security breach in its hot wallets — the biggest digital asset heist in history. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM attributed the attack to North Korea's Lazarus Group via a compromised engineer's laptop. Approximately $1.5 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated. Binance suspended all deposits and withdrawals and pledged to cover losses. Ethereum fell to $2,220. The hack compounds Friday's existing macro headwinds from the hot PCE data and December hike expectations.

desk.name: LNG
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) held near $32 per MMBtu as European TTF natural gas remained above €100 per MWh. Hormuz disruption continues to threaten Qatar's 106 million tonnes of annual LNG export capacity, and Qatari LNG flows through the strait have essentially halted with no large ships transiting since early September. Henry Hub eased to $3.10. The wide gap between US domestic and global spot markets persists, and below-average European storage heading into winter supports the bull case.

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated with CFR Southeast Asia around $1,100–1,300 per tonne, little changed on the week. Middle East FOB prices hold near $765. Hormuz disruption continues squeezing sulfuric acid supply chains — the essential input for copper leaching, phosphate fertilizer, and oil refining. Chinese sulfuric acid (98%) trades near 1,647 yuan per tonne per NBS data.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: Down from $396 in Jul · China port MOP ¥2,898
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds near $367 per tonne, little changed. Chinese domestic port MOP remains near 2,898 yuan per tonne. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions, routing through non-aligned buyers. Seasonal fertilizer demand in the Southern Hemisphere provides modest support.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: Off 105k high · flat week to Oct 26
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) held at 90,000 yuan per tonne through the week ending October 26, marking the first fully flat week after two consecutive weeks of sharp post-holiday declines from the 105,000-yuan high. SMM expects low-level sideways consolidation in the short term, though a second bottom test is possible if demand stays weak. Supply remains structurally tight under China's Document No. 46 export controls.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: China exports −94% since controls · domestic Ga ~¥1,740/kg
desk.sum: Gallium remains near a record $1,850 per kilogram outside China, up over 200% since early 2025. Chinese domestic gallium trades near 1,740 yuan per kilogram. Beijing's Document No. 46 export controls retain a presumption of denial for US end users, and the Busan truce's Document No. 72 suspension has not meaningfully restored exports. China produces about 98% of global gallium and 60% of germanium.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds near $5.02 per pound, slipping from $5.44 in 2024 as steel demand softens. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but the timing of large-scale adoption remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.sum: ICE cocoa eased to about $5,580 per tonne on Friday. Prices traded between $5,582 and $5,843 in the last two weeks of October, correcting from the August high of $6,821. Rising Ivory Coast arrivals and ICE inventories at a 2.25-year high continue to cap rallies, but El Niño forecasts affecting West African producers into 2027 provide support. The 1977 high of $5,104 acts as a pivot level.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.sum: Cobalt traded near $34,620 per tonne, little changed on the week but still down about 12% on the month. The DRC (70% of global mine supply) maintains export quotas of 96,600 tonnes per year to support prices, but the EV battery chemistry shift from NMC to LFP continues to structurally reduce demand. Glencore expects DRC exports to normalise in line with 2026 quotas.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate spot continued sliding toward ¥97,500 per tonne, with Guangzhou Futures Exchange contracts near ¥92,000. Prices have roughly halved from the mid-May peak above ¥200,000. The selloff accelerated after SMM restated Chinese stockpiles by adding 175,000 tonnes to inventory estimates, and mine restarts at Bald Hill and Finniss added supply. Goldman Sachs projects the global market flipping to a 444,000-tonne surplus by 2028.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades around $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), little changed. Southeast Asian supply remains tight with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by fungal leaf blight (Pestalotiopsis). Auto-sector demand remains solid, supported by replacement-tyre cycles.
